reneuro

A European energy system optimization model with an R interface.

r·en·euro provides a European energy system model built on energyRt. It was developed as teaching material for a modelling course, to replicate PyPSA-Eur, an established open model of the European power system, at several spatial resolutions.

Eleven models ship with the package, ready to solve — all built on 2025 weather and load (the europe-2025-sarah3-era5 cutout; measured ENTSO-E demand). They need neither Python nor a PyPSA-Eur clone, and are lazy-loaded, so they cost nothing until touched.

Four span spatial resolutions. Each models a single planning year — 2050 costs, the 2025 fleet as existing stock — resolved hour by hour within it:

model nodes snapshots how the regions were formed
pypsa_eur_5 5 one week (168 h) PyPSA-Eur k-means, Belgium only
pypsa_eur_5cp 5 one week (168 h) as above, copperplated
pypsa_eur_41 41 full year (8,760 h) PyPSA-Eur k-means
pypsa_eur_nuts3 1,035 full year (8,760 h) NUTS3 regions, weather ships separately

pypsa_eur_5, _5cp and _41 are reduced by PyPSA-Eur’s own cluster_network workflow and read straight into energyRt, so each is directly comparable to a PyPSA-Eur run at the same size.

pypsa_eur_nuts3 follows NUTS — Nomenclature des Unités Territoriales Statistiques, Eurostat’s hierarchy of European regions — rather than an algorithmic clustering, which is what lets the model be joined to published statistics. It is a source model rather than one to solve whole: its purpose is to supply a country or study area at full granularity, or a coarser continental model by aggregation. It covers the full year; its hourly weather is most of its size, so it ships as separate objects that attach_weather() puts back.

Planning across years

Seven more models take the 41-node system through 2050. Their calendar is the same full hourly year; what varies is the planning horizon:

model planning horizon what changes
pypsa_eur_41_2025 … _2050 one year each, 2025–2050 that horizon’s costs; the fleet aged by announced and assumed retirement
pypsa_eur_41v six five-year milestones, optimized together one model; the existing fleet split into 17 build-year vintages, plus an investable path per carrier

The _YYYY series answers “what does the system look like solved at a horizon”; pypsa_eur_41v optimizes the whole pathway at once, with per-vintage efficiency and retirement. All seven ship without weather — attach_weather(m, from = pypsa_eur_41) puts pypsa_eur_41’s profiles back, the same pattern pypsa_eur_nuts3 uses.

Coarser levels are derived, not shipped

NUTS0 and NUTS1 are a region aggregation of the NUTS3 model, so shipping them would store the same system twice more. pypsa_eur_nuts3 carries nuts_gs, so one call builds either:

m <- energyRt::aggregate_model_regions(pypsa_eur_nuts3, level = "nuts1")

Capacities and demand are summed, efficiencies and costs take a capacity-weighted mean, and corridors that fall inside one region are dropped. It takes a few seconds and gives 36 regions at NUTS0, 106 at NUTS1 and 289 at NUTS2.

Planned

pypsa_eur_nuts3v the vintaged build at NUTS3 resolution — next in line
pypsa_eur_250 PyPSA k-means at the size normally used for continental studies
transmission expansion the converter already maps extendable corridors (expand_transmission = TRUE); a shipped scenario is pending

The About article covers how each model was built, the four countries outside NUTS, and the region data that ships alongside.

Installation 

# install.packages("pak")
pak::pak("optimal2050/reneuro")

energyRt is not on CRAN; pak installs it from GitHub alongside reneuro. A solver is also required, and HiGHS through Julia or Python is the one to install — GLPK solves the five-node models below, but does not scale past them:

  • energyRt.org — documentation, reference and articles
  • Installation guide — R package, back ends and solvers
  • en_setup() — installs the Julia and Python dependencies from R

HiGHS can be used to solve sampled models (timeslices and/or regions) on an standard laptop, while full resolution models require commercial solvers, such as CPLEX or Gurobi.

Quick start 

library(reneuro)
library(energyRt)

# check the model
report(pypsa_eur_5)

scen <- interpolate_model(pypsa_eur_5, name = "be")
# GLPK at five nodes: this is the call that produced `be_solved`.
# Use solver_options$julia_highs (or $pyomo_highs) for anything larger.
scen <- write_script(scen, solver = solver_options$glpk)
scen <- read_solution(solve_scenario(scen, wait = TRUE))

getData(scen, "vObjective", merge = TRUE)$value

# quick look at the results
report(scen)

The solved scenario also ships as be_solved, so the results can be explored without a solver installed.

Contributing

Contributions are welcome. Issues and pull requests may be opened at github.com/optimal2050/reneuro. The package follows the optimal2050 conventions.

Licence

reneuro’s sources are Apache-2.0. It imports energyRt, which is AGPL-3, so a distribution of the two together is conveyed under AGPL-3. The shipped models inherit the licences of their inputs, chiefly ODbL-1.0 for OpenStreetMap transmission topology. Full detail, including data provenance, is in the About article and in NOTICE.

If you use reneuro in research, please cite it with citation("reneuro") and also cite PyPSA-Eur — see References.
